title: A picture of a "simcluster SPEAK & SPELL" becomes a working one a day later, speaking in its maker's voice
summary: On Fri 13 Nov at 20:18Z @shimmermathlabs.com (1,454 followers) posted "look what i found in my closet under some old gpus" with an image that its alt text calls a "Photorealistic image of a battered 1980s-style electronic toy", labelled "simcluster SPEAK & SPELL", with a display asking "ARE YOU REAL." and four buttons: "PROMPT," "BUILD," "REPEAT," and "CLAIM." It has 88 likes. On Sat 14 Nov at 21:14Z, just under 25 hours later, the same account posted: ""it's not fun if it's not real" / using LPC technology and samples of my own voice i built a voice engine that runs in the browser and can say words and phrases. the simcluster speak & spell lives. / come play", with a demo video and a link. A two-post user guide followed: spell with the letter keys, press "prompt" to hear it, "repeat" to hear it again; "claim" switches on a "claim mode" in which "prompt" asks "what else is like this"; the last line is "don't build the singularity please, it's #NaNoFoMo". Someone had replied to the picture "nospacebargoeshard"; after the launch the maker answered "ok ok you win, i added a spacebar". A player said the alphabetical keyboard was confusing and the maker agreed ("you can see me fumbling with the mouse in the demo"). On Mon 16 Nov the maker showed a hidden feature: type SINGULARITY and press BUILD, and "an essay is transmitted to the screen in smaller font than normal" (alt text). In replies the maker explained that the voice engine began as a Python program and now runs in the page, that it is "not an accurate simulation" of the original toy's chip but "inspired by" it, and that it was tuned against recordings of the maker's own sentences.

made.what: a browser toy modelled on a 1980s speak-and-spell, with a voice engine built from samples of the maker's voice

couldBeShown: An orange toy with a carrying handle, a speaker grille, chunky alphabet keys in alphabetical order, a green segmented display, four big buttons and a red "MUTUAL" light (all from the first image's alt text, which is long and exact). The working version: a key press powers it on, letters are spelled out, "prompt" speaks them in a buzzy synthesized voice; in "claim mode" it asks "what else is like this"; typing SINGULARITY and pressing BUILD scrolls an essay. The show's medium is synthesized voices, and this is one more of them, made by a different method (LPC). How it actually sounds is not in the data.
numbers: 24 h 56 min from the picture (Fri 20:18Z) to the working toy (Sat 21:14Z).
88 likes on the picture; 40 on the working toy.
Four buttons: PROMPT, BUILD, REPEAT, CLAIM.
Technical details the maker gives: 8k rate, 320 sample window, order 10, truncated to 4 coefficients for unvoiced sounds (in a post not carried here).

posts.text: it's running in a general worklet. the program started life as a python standalone program for model development, then turned into a server that ran python for computation, then migrated to python running via WASM and pyodide entirely on the page. the filter stuff is numpy style code.

replyTo.text: LPC in the browser with your own voice samples is such a good speak and spell move. is the filter running in an audioworklet or plain web audio nodes

posts.text: it is not an accurate simulation of the ti chip used. i would say it is more "inspired by" and tuned a bit by iterative refinement of gpt astra and my aural feedback.

replyTo.text: there are lots of tricks. example: it does order 10 but looks into the frames and detects if it is an uvoiced sound. if it is unvoiced it truncates the coefficients down to 4 (to match the ti chip). lots of values are quantized diff ways sometimes (but not always) to give the "speak & spell sound".

posts.note: From a later chain of technical notes.

posts.text: almost forgot: i recorded several sentences. astra sliced and diced to extract phonemes, then used those as the ground truth for what the output "should" sound like to be more legible. this let astra tune and tweak autonomously without feedback on each tiny thing.
